performers: Nanny Larsen-Todsen, soprano; Bayreuth Festival Orchestra; Karl Elmendorff
intro: Nanny Larsen-Todsen sings the Liebestod, “Mild und leise”, from Tristan und Isolde, WWV 90, in which Isolde looks at Tristan’s body and sees him smiling. Muted strings and harp figures accompany her, and the music closes in B major.

sections.label: A · Isolde’s first words, “Mild und leise”
sections.mNote: Bass clarinet and muted cellos accompany Isolde’s first quiet words.

sections.label: B · Harp figures beneath the soprano
sections.mNote: Harp figures and string tremolo accompany the soprano’s long phrases.

sections.label: Dev · Wind phrases over strings and harp
sections.mNote: Wind phrases rise over circling strings and harp.

sections.label: C · Piccolo above the soprano
sections.mNote: The piccolo and high violins play above sustained brass.

sections.label: Coda · Isolde’s last words, B major
sections.mNote: The harp continues after Isolde’s last words.

cues.title: Isolde’s first words, muted cellos
cues.text: “Mild und leise, wie er lächelt” — “Softly and gently, how he smiles.” Isolde’s first words rise above muted, divided cellos. The bass clarinet has a phrase of its own, and a clarinet and then the horns join it, while the violins rest.
cues.evidence: Wagner’s Act III text, sung by Isolde over Tristan’s body. Breitkopf & Härtel, Vorspiel und Isoldens Liebestod, plate Part. B. 1544, p. 14: bass clarinet, divided muted cellos, subsequent clarinet and horn entries. Own translation. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/13070.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Isolde’s address to the onlookers
cues.text: “Seht ihr, Freunde?” — “Do you see, friends?” Isolde asks the people around Tristan’s body to see what she sees. She describes his eyes opening, his heart swelling and his breath. Tristan has already died.
cues.evidence: Wagner’s libretto, Act III, Isolde’s final monologue; Breitkopf excerpt score, pp. 14–18. Own translation of ‘Seht ihr, Freunde?’ The preceding death of Tristan is described in the Act III synopsis at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tristan_und_Isolde.

cues.title: Harp arpeggios and string tremolos
cues.text: The harp enters with rising arpeggios over divided string tremolos. High flute phrases are held across the bar, and the soprano sings a slower, sustained line above the quicker notes of the orchestra.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score, pp. 18–22, harp entry and developing arpeggios, divided string tremolos, high flute phrases and sustained vocal writing.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Stage career, 1906–1928
cues.text: Larsen-Todsen began her stage career in Stockholm in 1906 as Agathe in Weber’s Der Freischütz, and later took on Wagner’s major soprano roles. In 1928 she sang Isolde at Bayreuth and recorded the role with Karl Elmendorff and the festival orchestra.
cues.evidence: Dr Anton Odelga, biographical note on Preiser LV 174; recording entry for ‘Mild und leise’, Columbia L 2206, 1928, Bayreuth Festival Orchestra, Karl Elmendorff. https://archive.org/download/nanny-larsen-todsen-preiser-lv-174-side-a/Larsen-Todsen%20Preiser%20%282%29.JPG.

cues.title: Rehearsal Hh, harp and winds
cues.text: At rehearsal Hh Isolde hears sounds swelling around her and wonders whether they are waves of air. The harp plays arpeggios up and down, and the strings play continuous quick figures. Above them the wind instruments repeat a broad rising phrase, with swells.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score, pp. 23–25, especially rehearsal Hh on p. 24: ‘mich umwallend, sind es Wellen sanfter Lüfte’, harp arpeggios, continuous string figures and repeated wind phrases with swells.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Piccolo above the voice
cues.text: The piccolo and first violins play high above Isolde. The harp plays wide arpeggios, and the brass hold sustained chords underneath. Her melody moves in long notes.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score, pp. 27–28, piccolo and high violin writing, wide harp arpeggios, sustained brass chords and Isolde’s long notes at ‘Welt-Atems wehendem All’.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final bars in B major
cues.text: Isolde’s last words are “höchste Lust” — “supreme bliss”. The harp continues after the voice stops. The closing music settles in B major, and the last arpeggios are followed by a held chord marked pianissimo.
cues.evidence: Wagner’s Act III text, final words of Isolde; own translation. Breitkopf score, pp. 29–30, harp continuation after the vocal release, final B-major chord, pp and fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Rising wind phrases over circling strings
transitions.from: B · Harp figures beneath the soprano
transitions.to: Dev · Wind phrases over strings and harp
transitions.how: The bass holds long notes beneath repeated rising phrases in the woodwind (rehearsal Hh). Trumpets and trombones sustain the harmony. The harp plays arpeggios up and down, and the strings continue their circling figures in quick notes. Each broad wind phrase swells and then falls back, and Isolde’s line continues through the successive phrases.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf score, pp. 23–25, rehearsal Hh: long bass notes, sustained brass, repeated woodwind phrases, string figures and harp arpeggios.

transitions.title: Harp continues to the final cadence
transitions.to: Coda · Isolde’s last words, B major
transitions.how: The high violin figures turn downwards and the brass grow softer. Harp arpeggios continue beneath Isolde’s last phrase, then beneath the orchestra alone. A sustained bass and increasingly quiet wind chords move towards B major. The harp stops, and the last chord is held under a fermata.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf score, pp. 29–30: descending violin figures, diminishing brass, harp continuation, final B-major cadence and fermata. The preserved section boundary marks the approach to this closing passage.

source.title: Wagner: Vorspiel und Isoldens Liebestod, with vocal part — Breitkopf & Härtel
source.locator: Printed pp. 14–30; broad score-proportion landmarks, not bar-synchronised entrances.

timeline.note: Opening span, p. 14: low tremolando strings support Isolde; bass clarinet and trombones enter softly.
Approximate first expansion, pp. 15–17: brighter woodwind and harp join the strings and voice.
Approximate middle span: woodwind responses and active inner strings accompany the continuing vocal line.
Broad accumulating span, pp. 24–27: harp, woodwind and strings keep playing while the brass reinforces the rises.
Late climactic region, pp. 27–28; the timestamp marks the strongest audio crest, not each instrumental entrance.
Final orchestral cadence, p. 30. The voice has finished; quiet wind and string lines move to the final chords. Cor anglais and timpani play at points within this closing section, not throughout it.

composer.epithet: Composer who placed the orchestra beneath the stage at Bayreuth, hidden from the audience.
facts: Theodor Weinlig, Leipzig, 1831; then the daily work of provincial opera houses
Dresden court conductor, 1843–49 · Bayreuth Festival founder, 1876
Wrote his own librettos; published essays on theatre, music and politics
Thirteen completed operas, including the four evenings of the Ring
composer.background:
In 1839 Richard Wagner and his wife Minna fled Riga ahead of their creditors and took a storm-battered ship to London. He was twenty-six, an opera conductor with two completed operas and no real success. The sea passage stayed with him. A story by Heinrich Heine about a captain condemned to sail for ever became Der fliegende Holländer; its overture begins over a bare fifth, with horns and bassoons playing against the storm music in the strings. The Wagners went on to Paris, where he made arrangements for publishers and tried to get his music staged.

He grew up in the theatre. Born in Leipzig in 1813, he lost his father as an infant and moved with his mother into the household of Ludwig Geyer, an actor and painter in Dresden. Wagner wanted to write plays before he knew how to write music. He heard Weber’s Der Freischütz and Beethoven’s symphonies, and in 1831 he took counterpoint lessons from Theodor Weinlig. Posts followed in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga. Die Feen was not performed, and Das Liebesverbot, his operatic version of Measure for Measure, failed after one performance in 1836. That year he married Minna, an actress.
